ety.text: From Middle English rollen, partly from Old French roller, roler, röeler, röoler, from Medieval Latin rotulāre (“to roll; to revolve”), from Latin rotula (“a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”); partly from Anglo-Latin rollāre, from the same ultimate source. Displaced native English welt and partially displaced English wallow.

chain.g: a roll, list, catalogue, schedule, record, a paper or parchment rolled up

ety.text: From Middle English rolle, from Old French rolle, role, roule, from Medieval Latin rotulus (“a roll, list, catalogue, schedule, record, a paper or parchment rolled up”); as such, it is a doublet of role and rotulus.

senses.d: To revolve by turning over and over; to move by turning on a horizontal axis; to impel forward with a revolving motion on a supporting surface.
ex: To roll a wheel, a ball, or a barrel.
The child will roll on the floor.

senses.d: To wrap (something) round on itself; to form into a spherical or cylindrical body by causing to turn over and over.
ex: To roll a sheet of paper; to roll clay or putty into a ball.
The cloth rolls unevenly; the snow rolls well.

senses.d: To bind or involve by winding, as with a bandage; to enwrap; often with up.
ex: To roll up the vase in bubble wrap.

senses.d: To drive, impel, or flow onward with a steady, wave-like motion.
ex: This river will roll its waters to the ocean.
The years roll on.

senses.d: To pour or trickle.
ex: Drops of sweat rolled down his face.

senses.d: To utter copiously, especially with sounding words; to utter with a deep sound; — often with forth, or out.
ex: To roll forth someone's praises; to roll out sentences.

senses.d: To press, level, spread, or form with a roller or rollers.
ex: to roll a field; to roll paste; to roll steel rails.
The pastry rolls well.

senses.d: To move upon rollers or wheels.
To tumble in gymnastics; to do a somersault.
To leave or begin a journey; sometimes with out.
ex: I want to get there early; let's roll.

senses.d: The act or result of rolling, or state of being rolled.
ex: the roll of a ball
Look at the roll of the waves.

senses.d: Something formed into a compact shape by being rolled up.
ex: a roll of banknotes

senses.d: A forward or backward roll in gymnastics; going head over heels. A tumble.
A heavy cylinder used to break clods.
One of a set of revolving cylinders, or rollers, between which metal is pressed, formed, or smoothed, as in a rolling mill.
ex: to pass rails through the rolls

senses.d: A swagger or rolling gait.
A heavy, reverberatory sound.
ex: Hear the roll of cannon.
There was a roll of thunder and the rain began to pour down.

senses.d: The uniform beating of a drum with strokes so rapid as scarcely to be distinguished by the ear.

The oscillating movement of a nautical vessel as it rotates from side to side, about its fore-and-aft axis, causing its sides to go up and down, as distinguished from the alternate rise and fall of bow and stern called pitching; or the equivalent in an aircraft.
The measure or extent to which a vessel rotates from side to side, about its fore-and-aft axis.
That which is rolled up.
ex: a roll of fat, of wool, paper, cloth, etc.

senses.d: A document written on a piece of parchment, paper, or other materials which may be rolled up; a scroll.
ex: Busy angels spread / The lasting roll, recording what we say.

senses.d: An official or public document; a register; a record.
A catalogue or list, (especially) one kept for official purposes.
ex: The roll of solicitors contains the names of all admitted solicitors of a jurisdiction.
Several people sued the state after finding out that they'd been removed from the voter rolls for having died, despite their not actually being dead.

senses.d: A food preparation comprising one or more ingredients wrapped in, e.g., flatbread, lettuce leaf, etc.
A quantity of cloth wound into a cylindrical form.
ex: a roll of carpeting; a roll of ribbon

senses.d: A cylindrical twist of tobacco.
A kind of shortened raised biscuit or bread, often rolled or doubled upon itself; see also bread roll.
A part; an office; a duty; a role.
A measure of parchments, containing five dozen.
ex: Parchement is sold by the dozen, and by the roll of five dozens.
